forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bradford forecasts £391m of exceptional support since 2023-24, against £570m planned
news_drafts.lead:
Bradford Council expects 2027-28 to be the first financial year since 2022-23 in which it can operate without exceptional financial support, which is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. Papers for the Executive meeting on 3 November put the cumulative support from 2023-24 onwards at £391m on the current forecast, against an original plan of £570m. The paper says the council "has relied upon cumulative EFS of £391 million to support its revenue budget".

By year, the support was £80m in 2023-24. In 2024-25 it came out at £120m, £20m below the original request of £140m. In 2025-26 it came out at £113m, which was £14.1m below the £127.1m requested. For 2026-27 the council forecasts £78m, against an original plan of £129m.

The paper says the council "is currently forecasting a return to a financially sustainable position from 2027-28, at which point reliance on EFS is no longer expected". It links that expectation to delivery of the recovery programme, the savings proposals in the report, and the additional funding expected from the Fair Funding review.

news_drafts.headline: Bradford Council's 2025-26 accounts: £113m overspend, usable reserves up £55m to £229.2m, clean audit opinion expected
news_drafts.lead:
Bradford Council ended 2025-26 with usable reserves of £229.2m, up £55.0m on the year, even though its day-to-day spending ran £113m over budget, the Governance and Audit Committee heard on 24 September. The council's statement of accounts, its formal annual accounts, says the overspend was £14m smaller than first forecast and was paid for through a capitalisation direction, government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so it can be funded by borrowing or asset sales. The accounts say part of the rise in reserves comes from earmarking costs funded that way. The general fund balance, the cushion for the unexpected, is £53.1m, or 3.5% of about £1.5bn of gross spending.

The council's external auditor, Forvis Mazars, anticipates an unqualified opinion, meaning a full sign-off, on the accounts. That is subject to remaining work, including investment property valuations, land and buildings indexation, pension liability work, capital grants and long-term borrowing balances. The council says no material changes were needed to its primary statements and that it has no audit backlog. Overall materiality, the level of error the auditor treats as significant, is £31.5m.

The accounts record a £23.7m net fall from revaluing buildings, park land and investment properties. Non-current assets fell £13.2m overall despite £79.4m of capital enhancements. The Executive's July 2026 decision not to proceed with the Square Lane project means £4.9m of abortive costs will be charged to day-to-day spending, taking usable reserves from £229.2m to £224.3m.

The council's pension scheme has assets of £3.1bn against liabilities of £2.2bn, a surplus of £871m. An accounting restriction known as the asset ceiling means no net pension asset appears on the balance sheet.

Separately, the West Yorkshire Pension Fund's audit report anticipates an unqualified opinion. Its auditor found a £60.9m understatement in hard-to-value investments, which management corrected, and left £30.3m of estimated further error unadjusted. A revised transaction report raised recorded purchases and sales by £842.4m after testing found the first did not match supporting evidence.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.headline: WYPF staff averaged 5.28 days of sickness absence per staff member for the year to 1 April 2026, against a Council average of 14.00 days.
findings.detail: The paper also reports a headcount of 242 (238 full time equivalent) and 31 starters against 20 leavers over the last 12 months. It says the IT restructure is intended to give resilience, efficiencies and cost benefits.
findings.matters: Sickness and turnover figures bear on the capacity and cost of a shared administration service, and the IT restructure is a staffing change other finance teams may be weighing.
findings.figures: 5.28 days per staff member (WYPF); 14.00 days (Council average); 242 headcount; 238 FTE; 31 starters; 20 leavers
findings.quote: For the year to 1 April 2026 the average number of days absence due to sickness is 5.28 days per staff member. This compares with the Council average of 14.00 days

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.headline: The contract for WYPF's pensions administration system, currently Civica's UPM platform, is due to expire in August 2028, and a tender invitation has recently been published.
findings.detail: The paper says the current contract ends in August 2028 and that the tender has recently been issued to interested bidders. No cost or bidder information is given.
findings.matters: Re-procurement of a pensions administration platform is a multi-year cost and change event that other councils and funds on UPM or similar systems will face on their own timelines.
findings.quote: The contract for the Pensions administration system is due to expire in August 2028.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.headline: The Pension Estimate KPI was met for 71.92% of cases against a 90% minimum target, which the paper attributes to a large volume of estimates for one early retirement scheme.
findings.detail: The paper identifies the cause as a large volume of estimates received from a local authority for an early retirement scheme. Across all work types, the total KPI met was 94.62%.
findings.matters: A single employer's early retirement exercise can swing service performance for a whole administration function, which matters to any council judging its own shared-service KPIs.
findings.figures: 1784 cases total; 1283 met; 71.92% met against 90% minimum target; overall total 94.62%
findings.quote: * Pension Estimate – Large volume of estimates received for an early retirement scheme from a local authority.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.headline: The Deferred Benefits Into Payment Quote KPI was met for 58.93% of cases against an 85% minimum target in the July to September 2026 period.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the miss partly to extra checks and individual record updates for members in scope for the McCloud remedy. WYPF says it is working towards a bulk McCloud update for deferred records.
findings.matters: McCloud remedy workload is a cost and resourcing pressure across LGPS funds, and a bulk update approach is one way other funds may handle the same backlog.
findings.figures: 2179 cases total; 1284 met; 58.93% met against 85% minimum target
findings.quote: Deferred Benefits Into Payment Quote - Was not met, partly due to the need to carry out additional checks and individual record updates for members in scope for McCloud remedy.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.headline: Bradford Council Internal Audit gave the LGPS Pensioner Payroll review a "partially effective" opinion, with three recommendations made and two implemented.
findings.detail: The paper states that most risks examined were effectively managed, but that the control environment would benefit from some enhancement. The third recommendation is still being discussed with HSBC.
findings.matters: A finance director at any council running a pensioner payroll would want to know which control areas auditors have flagged and how far the remediation has progressed.
findings.quote: It is audit’s opinion that the standard of control of identified risks in the system is partially effective.
